articles.author: Nisha Khot
articles.content: Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said , “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland. This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required. Continue reading...

articles.content: Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS ( Letters, 18 November ). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades. Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. articles.content: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.content: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers ? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference. articles.author: Cath Clarke
articles.content: Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24 This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo . His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe. AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them. Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the sea and surfing here, and a gentle tapping into surfing’s spiritual side; a handful of gorgeous scenes in a palette of mushroom brown and grey tell snippets of its origins in Polynesia. At heart, In Waves is an idealistic, emotional film, handling its subject delicately, avoiding too much of the rawness of grief. I can imagine older kids and teenagers falling deeply in love with it. Continue reading...
